newsitem.title: UK: CRICKET-Bowlers won test, not batsmen - Atherton.
newsitem.headline: CRICKET-Bowlers won test, not batsmen - Atherton.

text.p: CHRISTCHURCH, Feb 19 - English aggression with the ball paved the way for their exciting four-wicket win in the third and final cricket test against New Zealand, according to captain Mike Atherton.
England, needing 305 to wrap up the series, finished on 307 for six, with 12.2 overs to spare to make it back-to-back wins over New Zealand.

But while Atherton took the limelight with an outstanding batting display, and undefeated seventh wicket pair John Crawley and Dominic Cork earned plaudits for their fighting performance in the final session yesterday, the skipper claimed the bowlers set up the victory.
At the halfway point in the test, New Zealand held a 118-run first innings lead.
However they were bowled out for 186 in their second innings and England got to their target with skilful batting over the last day-and-a-half.
"We didn't play so well over the first two days and that's what made it difficult for us," Atherton said last night.
"The key thing was coming out so aggressively in the second innings to bowl them out. That was the key to winning the match.
"When you've got a deficit of 120 it's easy to say we're second favourites.
"The opposition just build a lead without you dictating terms and I was very keen for us to dictate terms in the second innings.
"We just wanted to show the opposition that we felt we could still win the game."
The result was that New Zealand slumped to 95 for six at stumps on the third day and had lost all their earlier momentum.

Atherton then stepped forward, following his first innings 94 not out with a fine 118 -- his fourth hundred against New Zealand and 11th in all tests -- while Crawley and Cork put on 76 at the finish to shut the door on the Kiwis.
For a time yesterday afternoon, New Zealand fought their way back with three wickets in 16 balls.
Atherton admitted he was edgy at that point.
"I don't like watching in those circumstances," Atherton said.
"There was a little group of four or five down on a sofa in the changing room going through about 30 packets of fags. It was fairly tense."
Teenage left arm spinner Daniel Vettori was ready for a rest last night.
He was New Zealand's crucial bowler in England's second innings and toiled determinedly for 57 overs, taking four for 97.
But he couldn't make the final push through the England middle order, and New Zealand suffered for not having veteran offspinner Dipak Patel working in tandem with the 18-year-old.
Instead medium pacer Nathan Astle was asked to tie up an end for 28 overs while two of the fast-medium bowlers, Geoff Allott and Chris Cairns were used for just 22.4 overs.
"I am a little bit tired, but I expected to bowl that many overs," Vettori said last night.
"I tried to guts it out but it was hard work.
"It was nice being part of the team effort. I enjoyed bowling all those overs. I just wanted to do as well as I could for the team."
New Zealand coach Steve Rixon conceded England deserved their win, but he was proud of the commitment shown by his team.
"The best side won. But we played good competitive cricket and were up there for a good percentage of it," he said.
"It's the way I want us to play."
Rixon said it wouldn't be difficult picking the New Zealand team up again for the one-day series against England, starting here on Thursday.
"If we'd been comprehensively beaten, as we were in the second test at Wellington, then it would be a genuine problem," Rixon added.
"What it has done is stagnate our progress. This was an important game for us. If we had won we would have gone into the one-dayers very, very confident.
"Now we have to make the one-dayers as the launching pad and go into the Sri Lankan tests with the same sort of confidence."
Sri Lanka will play two tests and three one-day internationals after the England tour is finished.
